vignette:
The Weight of the Intersection

Bernard is a 67-year-old man who has spent the better part of four decades shaping the lives of children as a school principal in a mid-sized regional town. He is the kind of man who arrives early and leaves late, who knows every student by name, and who has always prided himself on being steady — the calm center around which everything else turns. His wife, Elaine, describes him as someone who has never needed much from anyone. That changed fourteen months ago on a Tuesday afternoon in late autumn.

Bernard was driving home from a district meeting, traveling through a familiar intersection he had crossed thousands of times. A delivery truck ran a red light at speed and struck the driver's side of his car. The vehicle spun, rolled, and came to rest against a power pole. Bernard was conscious throughout — he remembers the sound of metal folding, the strange stillness afterward, the smell of something burning, and the absolute certainty, in those seconds, that he was going to die. He did not. He sustained a fractured collarbone, three broken ribs, and lacerations to his face and left arm. Physically, he recovered within a few months. In every other sense, he has not.

In the weeks following the accident, Bernard attributed his sleeplessness and agitation to pain and the disruption of his routine. He returned to work as soon as his body allowed, telling himself and Elaine that keeping busy was the best medicine. But the intersection would not leave him. It arrives without invitation — while he is reviewing student files, while he is speaking at assembly, while he is lying beside his wife in the dark. The sound of the impact replays with a fidelity that still shocks him. He finds himself gripping the edge of his desk when it comes, waiting for it to pass.

He no longer drives through that intersection. He has constructed an elaborate alternate route that adds twenty minutes to his commute each way, and he has told no one at school why. When a colleague once suggested they take a shortcut through the area, Bernard manufactured an excuse so quickly it surprised even him. He does not drive after dark if he can avoid it, and when he must, he finds himself scanning every approaching vehicle with a vigilance that leaves him exhausted by the time he arrives anywhere.

At school, Bernard functions — but those who know him well have noticed something flattened in him. He still attends every meeting, still writes his thoughtful notes to staff, still stands at the front gate each morning. But the warmth that once animated him surfaces less reliably now. He finds it difficult to feel genuinely present with his students, and this troubles him perhaps more than anything else. He used to find the job replenishing. Now he moves through it as though behind glass.

At home, Elaine bears the quieter weight of his withdrawal. He wakes most nights between two and four, and rather than disturb her, he sits in the kitchen with a cup of tea he rarely finishes. He has become irritable in ways that embarrass him — snapping at her over small things, then feeling a wash of shame that he cannot quite articulate. He does not tell her about the nightmares because he does not want to frighten her, and also because putting them into words feels like inviting them to solidify.

Bernard came to therapy at Elaine's gentle insistence, and also, he admits, because he is approaching retirement and the thought of having less structure — fewer obligations to organize his days around — fills him with a dread he cannot fully explain. He sits in the chair with his hands folded in his lap, precise and composed, and speaks carefully. But when he describes the moment of impact, his voice loses its steadiness in a way that seems to surprise him every time, as though he had hoped, once more, that it might not.
